article.headline: The Straight Line That Ate Forty Years of Panic
article.lede: One Bloomberg screenshot, one quiet provocation: on a log scale, the S&P 500's 40-fold rise since 1985 looks less like a rocket ship than a well-behaved trend line. The chart does not prove the market is cheap. It does ask whether the parabola you see on TV is mostly an arithmetic illusion.
article.body:
There is a trick of the eye that haunts every financial television segment. Pull up the S&P 500 on a standard, *linear* chart — one in which equal distances represent equal point moves — and the recent decade looks nearly vertical. The index sat at 182 in September 1985. It closed April 2026 near 7,230. Drawn on ordinary graph paper, that 40-fold gain appears to accelerate toward some terminal cliff. The chart that @BergMilton posted on Bloomberg Terminal, and mirrored on TradingView, swaps the vertical axis for a logarithmic one: equal distances now represent equal *percentage* moves. The line from 1985 to today becomes, almost uncannily, straight.

The mathematics here is not controversial. A market compounding at a roughly constant annual rate — the S&P 500 has averaged close to ten percent per year in nominal terms over the modern era — will look exponential on a linear chart and linear on a log chart. The slope of the log chart encodes the compound growth rate; deviations from that slope encode periods of excess or deficiency. Viewed this way, the 2000 dot-com peak shows as a genuine bulge above trend, as does the 2021-22 post-pandemic surge. The intervening crashes restore the line. The current reading, sitting near the top of that channel, is elevated — but not uniquely so.

This is, admittedly, a congenial framing for bulls. The **Shiller CAPE** — the cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio, which smooths reported earnings over ten years to strip out the business cycle — stood at roughly 40.9 as of early May 2026. That is among the two highest readings in recorded history, matched only by the final months of the dot-com bubble in 1999-2000. Robert Shiller's own model, applied to current levels, implies total returns averaging around 1.3 percent per year over the next decade, barely above inflation. One chart says "steady trend"; another says "priced for perfection." Both are true simultaneously, because they measure different things: the log-scale chart captures nominal price history, while the CAPE measures the relationship between price and earnings power. A market can track its exponential growth channel while still being grotesquely expensive relative to what companies actually earn.

The monetary backdrop sharpens the tension. The Federal Reserve held its benchmark rate at 3.5–3.75 percent in April 2026, pausing a gentle cutting cycle that began in late 2024. Jerome Powell's term expires in mid-May 2026, adding an unusual overlay of institutional uncertainty to the policy picture. Higher real rates, the standard argument runs, compress the *present value* of future earnings — the denominator in every valuation model. That the market has continued rising alongside still-elevated rates is either a sign of genuine earnings momentum (AI infrastructure spending is real; hyperscalers have committed over $200 billion in capex for 2026) or a sign that investors have simply stopped discounting at any rate that history would recognize as sane.

What the log chart does most usefully is restore humility in both directions. It reminds the reflexive bear that what looks like a bubble on the evening news may be nothing more than arithmetic: a healthy compound-growth machine photographed in the wrong coordinate system. And it reminds the complacent bull that mean reversion is equally visible on the same chart — the 2000 and 2008 drawdowns look every bit as dramatic in log space as they do on a linear one, just proportionally accurate rather than exaggerated. The S&P 500 currently trades roughly 83 percent above its modern-era log-linear trend, or about 2.3 standard deviations rich, depending on where you set the regression's start date. The line is straight. The index is not on it.

Perhaps the cleanest use of the log-scale argument is rhetorical: it is a scalpel for separating the question of *structural trend* from the question of *current valuation*. The former is reassuring. The latter is not. Conflating the two — as headlines do constantly, in both bubble-calling and bubble-denying directions — is the original sin of financial punditry. @BergMilton's two-word post ("WE prefer") makes no valuation claim at all. It just changes the lens, and lets the reader decide what is distortion and what is data.

concepts.definition: A chart axis on which equal distances represent equal percentage changes rather than equal point changes, making compound growth appear as a straight line rather than an accelerating curve.

The cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio, developed by economist Robert Shiller, which divides the S&P 500's price by the average of the prior ten years of real (inflation-adjusted) earnings to smooth out business-cycle distortions.
The tendency of an asset's price or valuation metric to drift back toward its long-run average over time, implying that extreme readings — high or low — are unlikely to persist indefinitely.
A chart on which equal vertical distances represent equal absolute point moves, causing a compounding asset to appear to accelerate exponentially even if its growth rate is constant.

article.fact_check: CAPE of ~40.9 confirmed via multpl.com as of May 4, 2026. SPX closing level of 7,230.12 matches Bloomberg OCR. S&P 500 YTD return of ~5.1% as of May 1, 2026 per Slickcharts. Fed funds target 3.5–3.75% confirmed via FOMC April 2026 decision. 83% above log-linear trend and 2.3 standard deviations from currentmarketvaluation.com (data through Dec 31, 2025).
article.thread_summary: Single-post observation by @BergMilton accompanied by a Bloomberg Terminal screenshot of SPX (1985–2026, last 7230.12) and a TradingView monthly chart. The post argues, by implication, that log-scale charting reveals a market in steady long-run trend rather than parabolic bubble territory.

ticker_spy.name: SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust
ticker_spy.blurb: The oldest and largest U.S. equity exchange-traded fund, launched in January 1993 by State Street Global Advisors as a vehicle to track the S&P 500 Index — a market-capitalisation-weighted benchmark of 500 large U.S. companies maintained by S&P Dow Jones Indices. SPY holds all constituent stocks in proportion to their index weight, with Apple, Microsoft, NVIDIA, Amazon and Meta typically constituting the top five positions. It trades continuously during market hours with daily volume in the hundreds of millions of shares, making it the world's most liquid single-listed equity security by dollar volume. Expense ratio: 0.0945% annually. SPY is often used as a proxy for 'the market' in both retail portfolios and institutional hedging strategies.
ticker_spy.recent: The S&P 500 closed at approximately 7,230 on May 1, 2026, representing a YTD gain of roughly 5.1% for 2026. The index's Shiller CAPE ratio stood near 40.9 as of early May 2026 — among the two highest readings in recorded history and exceeded only briefly during the 1999-2000 dot-com peak. The Federal Reserve held its benchmark rate at 3.5–3.75% at its April 2026 meeting, maintaining a pause in the cutting cycle that began in late 2024.
